unit.title: Angles and Constructions
unit.blurb: Corresponding and alternate angles on parallel lines, the exterior angle of a triangle, and ruler-and-compasses constructions.
unit.subject: maths

O1.t: Recognise corresponding, alternate and vertically opposite angles on parallel lines and use them to find angles.

O2.t: Use the fact that the exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles.

O3.t: Construct perpendicular bisectors, angle bisectors and triangles with ruler and compasses.

p: Two straight rails are parallel. A road crosses them at an angle, making a **58°** angle with the first rail.
What angles does the road make with the second rail? Which angles are equal, and why? Try it before you read on.
Vertically opposite angles are equal; angles on a straight line add to 180°.

p2: In the diagram a = e and b = f (corresponding); d = f and c = e (alternate); d + e = 180° and c + f = 180° (co-interior).

p: The facts work both ways: if corresponding (or alternate) angles are equal, the lines **are** parallel.

lesson.t: How do I find angles with parallel lines?
p: Step 1: Mark the parallel lines (arrows) and the transversal.
Step 2: Find a known angle and look for F, Z or C shapes linking it to the one you want.
Step 3: Use: corresponding = alternate (equal); co-interior add to 180°; straight line 180°; vertically opposite equal.
Step 4: Write the reason next to every angle.

sections.title: The exterior angle of a triangle

p: A carpenter extends the bottom edge of a triangular roof truss. Inside angles at the two far corners are **35°** and **75°**.
What angle does the roof make with the extended beam outside the third corner? Is there a shortcut? Try it before you read on.
The angles in a triangle add up to 180°.

qq.prompt: Two angles are 35° and 75°. Third angle?

p: If one side of a triangle is extended, the angle between the extension and the next side is an **exterior angle**.
Interior angles a, b, c: a + b + c = 180°. At C, c + exterior = 180° (straight line). So **exterior angle = a + b** – the sum of the two **interior opposite** angles.
Find an exterior angle from the two opposite interior angles in one step, or find a missing interior angle: if the exterior angle is 128° and one opposite angle is 50°, the other is 128 − 50 = 78°.
Remember the exterior angle is NOT equal to the angle next to it – they add to 180°.

qq.prompt: Interior opposite angles are 48° and 61°. Exterior angle?

errs.fb: That is the interior angle next to it.

lesson.t: How do I use the exterior angle fact?
p: Step 1: Identify the exterior angle (between a side and an extended side).
Step 2: Find the two interior angles NOT next to it.
Step 3: Exterior = sum of those two; or rearrange to find a missing one.
Step 4: Check: exterior + adjacent interior = 180°.

captions: A carpenter builds a triangular roof frame, and extends the bottom beam past one corner.
The inside angles at the other two corners are 35 degrees and 75 degrees.
What is the angle outside, between the roof and the extended beam?
Pause the video and work it out.
The third inside angle is 180 minus 35 minus 75, which is 70 degrees.
The outside angle is on a straight line with it, so it is 180 minus 70, which is 110 degrees.
But look: 35 plus 75 is also 110.
Is that a shortcut?
Remember: the angles inside a triangle add up to 180 degrees.
If two angles are 35 and 75, the third is 70 degrees.
If you extend one side of a triangle, the angle between the extension and the next side is called an exterior angle.
The interior angles a, b and c add up to 180.
And c plus the exterior angle e also make 180, because they are on a straight line.
So the exterior angle equals a plus b.
The exterior angle is the sum of the two interior angles opposite it.
Your turn.
The two opposite interior angles are 20 degrees and 90 degrees.
What is the exterior angle?
Pause the video and try it.
The exterior angle is the sum of the two opposite interior angles.
20 plus 90 is 110 degrees.
Remember: the exterior angle and the interior angle next to it add up to 180, not the same value.
Here is the method.
Step 1: find the exterior angle.
It is between a side and an extended side.
Step 2: find the two interior angles that are not next to it.
Step 3: the exterior angle equals their sum.
Or subtract to find a missing interior angle.
Step 4: check that the three interior angles add up to 180.
An exterior angle is 140 degrees.
One opposite interior angle is 85 degrees.
Find the other one.
140 minus 85 is 55.
The other angle is 55 degrees.
Your turn.
An exterior angle is 150 degrees, and one opposite interior angle is 72 degrees.
Find the other.
Pause and work it out.
150 equals 72 plus the other angle.
150 minus 72 is 78 degrees.
The opposite interior angles are 2 x and 3 x.
The exterior angle is 125 degrees.
Find x.
5 x equals 125, so x equals 25.
The angles are 50 degrees and 75 degrees.
An isosceles triangle has a top angle of 40 degrees.
Find the exterior angle at a base corner.
The two base angles are equal: 180 minus 40 is 140, and half of 140 is 70.
The exterior angle at a base corner is 40 plus 70, which is 110 degrees.
In triangle A B C, angle A is 50 degrees and angle B is 60 degrees.
Ruby finds the exterior angle at C.
Which line goes wrong first?
Line 2 is wrong.
The exterior angle and angle C are on a straight line, so they add up to 180.
They are not equal.
The exterior angle is 50 plus 60, which is 110 degrees.
A cyclist rides round a triangular route.
At each corner she turns through an exterior angle.
By the time she is back at the start, she has turned all the way round once.
So the three exterior angles of any triangle add up to 360 degrees.
One last question.
What is the exterior angle of an equilateral triangle?
Pause the video and answer.
Each interior angle is 60 degrees.
The exterior angle is 60 plus 60, which is 120 degrees.
And 3 times 120 is 360.
To remember: an exterior angle is made by extending one side of a triangle.
The exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior angles opposite it.
The exterior angle and the interior angle next to it add up to 180 degrees.
You can prove it with the angle sum of a triangle, and a straight line.

Compasses draw arcs: every point on an arc is the same distance from the centre.

p: **Perpendicular bisector of AB** (cuts AB in half at 90°): set compasses to more than half of AB; draw arcs from A and from B above and below; join the two crossing points. Every point on it is the same distance from A and B – the well goes on this line!
**Angle bisector** (cuts an angle in half): from the vertex draw an arc cutting both arms; from those two points draw equal arcs that cross; join the vertex to the crossing.

captions: Two villages want to dig a new well.
It must be exactly the same distance from both villages.
One point that works is halfway between them.
But there are many more.
Where are all the points that are the same distance from two places?
What shape do the points that are equally far from two villages make?
Pause the video and choose.
They make a straight line.
It goes through the halfway point, at right angles to the line joining the villages.
It is called the perpendicular bisector.
Bisector means it cuts the line in half.
Perpendicular means it meets it at 90 degrees.
Remember: compasses draw arcs.
Every point on an arc is the same distance from its centre.
That distance is the radius.
You can construct a triangle accurately from different starting facts.
With three sides, called S S S, draw one side.
Then draw arcs from each end with the other two lengths.
With two sides and the angle between them, S A S, use a ruler and a protractor.
With two angles and the side between them, A S A, measure both angles.
And for a right-angled triangle, R H S, draw the right angle, then use an arc for the longest side, the hypotenuse.
Your turn.
You are given three sides.
Which kind of construction is that?
Pause the video and choose.
Three sides is S S S: side, side, side.
To construct the perpendicular bisector of A B, open the compasses to more than half of A B.
Draw arcs from A, above and below the line.
Keep the same width.
Draw arcs from B, so they cross the first arcs.
Join the two crossing points.
Every point on this line is the same distance from A and from B.
To bisect an angle, draw an arc from the vertex, O, that crosses both arms.
From the two crossing points, draw two equal arcs that cross each other.
Join the vertex to that crossing point.
The angle is cut exactly in half.
Every point on this line is the same distance from both arms.
Here is the method.
Step 1: make a quick sketch with the measurements.
Step 2: draw the first line accurately with a ruler.
Step 3: keep the compass width fixed when you draw matching arcs.
Step 4: leave all your arcs showing, and check by measuring.
Construct triangle A B C with A B equal to 7 centimetres, B C equal to 5 centimetres, and A C equal to 6 centimetres.
Draw A B, 7 centimetres long.
Set the compasses to 6 centimetres and draw an arc from A.
Then set them to 5 centimetres and draw an arc from B.
C is where the arcs cross.
Join A C and B C.
A lamp must be the same distance from the two walls of a corner.
Where should it go?
Points that are equally far from two lines that meet are on the angle bisector.
So the lamp goes on the bisector of the corner angle.
Your turn.
Points equally far from two lines that meet lie on which construction?
Pause and choose.
Equally far from two lines that meet means the angle bisector.
Equally far from two points means the perpendicular bisector.
Max constructs the perpendicular bisector of A B.
Which line goes wrong first?
Line 2 is wrong.
Both arcs must have the same radius.
Otherwise the line does not cut A B in half.
Keep the compasses at 5 centimetres for both arcs.
Phone networks use the same idea.
A phone usually connects to the nearest mast.
The boundary between two masts' areas is the perpendicular bisector of the line joining them.
Maps made of these boundaries are called Voronoi diagrams.
They are also used to plan school catchment areas and delivery zones.
One last question.
The perpendicular bisector of a 10 centimetre line crosses it how far from each end?
Pause the video and answer.
It cuts the line in half.
Half of 10 is 5.
It crosses 5 centimetres from each end.
To remember: you can construct triangles from S S S, S A S, A S A or R H S.
Perpendicular bisector: equal arcs from both ends of the line.
Angle bisector: an arc from the vertex, then two equal arcs.
Keep your arcs, and check by measuring.
Great work! Now practise lesson 5.3 on Camday.
